name: Tazarotenic acid

lead: Tazarotenic acid is what the body makes from tazarotene, a prescription topical retinoid used for acne, psoriasis and photodamage. The payoff people want is fewer wrinkles, even tone and smoother texture; some forum users describe tazarotene as stronger than tretinoin.

Skin and blood esterases convert tazarotene to tazarotenic acid, which binds retinoic acid receptors, selectively RAR-beta and RAR-gamma, altering skin-cell growth and differentiation. A 12-month trial of tazarotene cream showed improvement in wrinkles and pigmentation versus vehicle. No studies have tested the acid alone.

paras: People encounter it only through tazarotene, a prescription cream or gel. Photoaging changes in trials built over months of regular use.
Irritation is the most common effect of the parent drug. It is contraindicated in pregnancy and is prescription-only in the US.

angle.text: Tazarotenic acid is the active form that prescription tazarotene converts into on skin, where it binds retinoic acid receptors to boost renewal and smooth wrinkles and pigmentation. A 12-month trial covers the parent drug; the acid alone is not sold.

lead: Tazarotenic acid is the active metabolite of tazarotene, a prescription topical retinoid. Tazarotene is a prodrug: after it is applied to the skin, esterase enzymes rapidly remove its ethyl ester group, producing the free acid that binds retinoic acid receptors [1][2][3]. It is not sold as a separate product; people encounter it through tazarotene (brands such as Tazorac, Arazlo and Fabior) [3].

Tazarotenic acid binds retinoic acid receptors (RARs) but not retinoid X receptors, and in laboratory assays it is selective for the RAR-beta and RAR-gamma subtypes [4][1]. Tazarotene is approved in the United States for acne, plaque psoriasis and, in some formulations, photodamage, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy [3].

In forum discussion, tazarotene is sometimes described as a stronger alternative to tretinoin for skin texture and anti-aging. No published study has tested tazarotenic acid as a stand-alone cosmetic ingredient; the human evidence concerns the parent drug.
infobox: Active metabolite of a topical retinoid (tazarotene)
Parent drug is Rx-only; contraindicated in pregnancy [3]

paras: Tazarotene belongs to the acetylenic retinoids, a class whose structure resists isomerization. Its free acid, tazarotenic acid, binds RARs and not RXRs, and gene-activation assays indicate selectivity for the RAR-beta and RAR-gamma subtypes [4][1]. Through these receptors it is described as slowing keratinocyte proliferation and promoting differentiation, and reviews also discuss comedolytic and anti-inflammatory properties of topical retinoids [5][3].

After topical application, only a few percent of the dose reaches the stratum corneum and viable epidermis, and a review of the drug's pharmacokinetics describes limited absorption into the bloodstream, with less than about 6% of the applied dose absorbed [6][7]. Tazarotene is converted by esterases in human blood and liver to tazarotenic acid [2]. Tazarotenic acid is then further metabolized, with cytochrome P450 2C8 and flavin-containing monooxygenases implicated in humans [8]. Over 99% is bound to plasma proteins and it is eliminated in urine and feces [3].
No studies found of tazarotenic acid administered on its own. Human trials have tested its parent drug, tazarotene.

In a 24-week double-blind trial of 563 people with facial photodamage, followed by a 28-week open-label extension, 0.1% tazarotene cream produced significantly more improvement than vehicle in fine wrinkling, mottled hyperpigmentation, lentigines and other signs; improvement had not plateaued by week 52. Twenty of 283 tazarotene-treated participants and 1 of 280 vehicle participants stopped because of adverse events, and plasma tazarotenic acid stayed at or below 0.71 ng/mL [9]. Pooled results of two vehicle-controlled trials examined 0.1% tazarotene cream in facial acne [10]. Registered trials have also looked at tazarotene in cutaneous T-cell lymphoma and scalp psoriasis [11][12].

Skin irritation (redness, itching, burning) is the most commonly reported effect of tazarotene and tends to rise with concentration [3]. A review of tazarotene safety concluded that systemic exposure is minimal and found no association with contact sensitization, phototoxicity or carcinogenicity [7]. Tazarotene is nonetheless labelled as contraindicated in pregnancy, a position based on animal studies [3].
Researchers have developed nanoparticle formulations of tazarotene intended to deliver it to hair follicles in inflammatory skin disease [13].

lore.intro: Tazarotenic acid is rarely named in community discussion; posts focus on tazarotene itself as a potent prescription retinoid for skin texture and aging.

Tazarotene creams approved; later foam (2012) and lotion (2019) [3].
